'''Andrew Kasarskis''' (born November 2, 1972) is an American biologist. He is the Chief Data Officer (CDO) at [http://www.Sema4.com Sema4].<ref name="Becker's Health IT">{{cite web|url=https://www.beckershospitalreview.com/healthcare-information-technology/4-hospital-execs-who-recently-left-their-roles-for-digital-health-companies.html |title=4 hospital execs who recently left their roles for digital health companies |access-date=2021-06-25}}</ref> He was previously CDO and an Executive Vice President (EVP) at the [[Mount Sinai Health System]] in New York City and, before that, vice chair of the Department of Genetics and Genomic Sciences and Co-director of the [[Icahn Institute for Genomics and Multiscale Biology]] at the [[Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai]].<ref name="icahn.mssm">{{cite web|url=http://icahn.mssm.edu/profiles/andrew-kasarskis |title=Andrew Kasarskis - Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai |publisher=Icahn.mssm.edu |access-date=2013-06-10}}</ref> Kasarskis is known for taking a network-based approach to biology and for directing the first medical school class offering students the opportunity to fully sequence and analyze their own genomes.<ref name="genomeweb">{{cite web|author=Nicholas Tatonetti |url=http://www.genomeweb.com/sequencing/qa-mount-sinais-andrew-kasarskis-teaching-students-how-analyze-their-own-genomes |title=Q&A: Mount Sinai's Andrew Kasarskis on Teaching Students how to Analyze their Own Genomes &#124; Clinical Sequencing News &#124; Sequencing |date=October 24, 2012 |publisher=GenomeWeb |access-date=2013-06-10}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==

Kasarskis completed bachelor's degrees in chemistry and biology at the [[University of Kentucky]] in 1992. In 1998, he completed his PhD in [[Molecular and Cell Biology|molecular and cell biology]] at the [[University of California, Berkeley]], under the supervision of Kathryn Anderson.<ref name="icahn.mssm" />

== Career and research ==

Throughout his career in industry and academia, Kasarskis' research has focused on the use of genetic and genomic data together with high-performance computing and advanced analytical tools to address biomedical needs and improve clinical treatment.

After completing his PhD in 1998, Kasarskis worked at [[Stanford University]] for two years, contributing to the development of various genome databases. In 2000, he entered industry, working in [[computational biology]] at DoubleTwist and later Rosetta Inpharmatics (acquired by Merck Research Laboratories). His work there centered on generating and mining complex biological data sets and using that information to build, predict, and model human disease. Kasarskis also worked for [[Sage Bionetworks]] and [[Pacific Biosciences]] before returning to academia.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.stanford.edu/class/biomedin206/bios_2010.html |title=BIOMEDIN 206: Informatics in Industry - Stanford University |publisher=Stanford.edu |access-date=2013-06-10}}</ref>

In 2011, Kasarskis became Vice Chair of the Department of Genetics and Genomic Sciences at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai and Co-director, along with [[Eric Schadt]], of the Icahn Institute for Genomics and Multiscale Biology, where Kasarskis's research focuses on improving health outcomes through better [[data mining]], and his research program includes sequencing-based pathogen surveillance; [[pharmacogenomics]]; electronic health records; and [[systems biology]] of sleep, behavior, and stress.<ref name="icahn.mssm" /> In 2019, Kasarskis was appointed Chief Data Officer and Executive Vice President of Mount Sinai Health System,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.mountsinai.org/about/newsroom/2019/mount-sinai-accelerates-datadriven-discovery-and-patient-care-with-new-chief-data-officer-role|title=Mount Sinai Accelerates Data-driven Discovery and Patient Care with New Chief Data Officer Role {{!}} Mount Sinai - New York|website=Mount Sinai Health System|language=en-US|access-date=2019-09-09}}</ref> where he leads efforts to improve clinical data infrastructure<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.genomeweb.com/informatics/qa-mount-sinai-chief-data-officer-andrew-kasarskis-his-new-role|title=Q&A: Mount Sinai Chief Data Officer Andrew Kasarskis on New Role|website=GenomeWeb|date=June 26, 2019|language=en-us|access-date=2019-09-09}}</ref> and leverage data to improve patient outcomes while accelerating research and innovation.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.mountsinai.org/about/newsroom/2019/mount-sinai-accelerates-datadriven-discovery-and-patient-care-with-new-chief-data-officer-role|title=Mount Sinai Accelerates Data-driven Discovery and Patient Care with New Chief Data Officer Role {{!}} Mount Sinai - New York|website=Mount Sinai Health System|language=en-US|access-date=2019-09-09}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.beckershospitalreview.com/hospital-executive-moves/mount-sinai-health-system-selects-first-chief-data-officer-6-things-to-know.html|title=Mount Sinai Health System selects first chief data officer: 6 things to know|website=www.beckershospitalreview.com|access-date=2019-09-09}}</ref>

Kasarskis is known for directing the first graduate course that allowed medical and PhD students to fully sequence and analyze their own genomes, along with co-instructors Michael Linderman, George Diaz, Ali Bashir, and Randi Zinberg. He has said that courses like this will be critical for training teams of people capable of performing this type of analysis in a medical setting. He chose [[whole genome sequencing]] because he expects the more limited [[exome sequencing]] will not be a relevant technological approach in the long term.<ref name="genomeweb" />

Kasarskis has called for improvements to [[informed consent]] protocols in patient research based on the concept that studies involving DNA cannot fully be made anonymous. He was quoted in the journal Nature saying, "We need to move beyond an assumption that you cannot be identified from the data that exist about you and really work to make sure that we're protecting people's rights in ways that allow us to use the data that are out there for individuals' and researchers' benefit."<ref>{{cite journal |url=http://www.nature.com/news/open-data-project-aims-to-ease-the-way-for-genomic-research-1.10507 |title=Open-data project aims to ease the way for genomic research |journal=Nature News |publisher=Nature.com |date=2012-04-25 |access-date=2013-06-10|doi=10.1038/nature.2012.10507 |last1=Check Hayden |first1=Erika |s2cid=211728919 |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

In 2019, Kasarskis joined a five-year collaborative study with Mount Sinai Health System, Sanofi, and Sema4, aimed to provide insights into the biological mechanisms of asthma using diverse data sets such as clinical data, genomics, immunological environmental, and sensor data from devices to carryout advanced network modeling of the disease. Kasarskis reported that understanding the molecular basis of clinical subtypes of asthma in the study would enable better management of asthma and could provide opportunities to discover new treatments for the disease.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.mountsinai.org/about/newsroom/2018/sanofi-sema4-mount-sinai-collaborate-on-largest-asthma-study-of-its-kind|title=Sanofi, Sema4, Mount Sinai Collaborate on Largest Asthma Study of Its Kind {{!}} Mount Sinai - New York|website=Mount Sinai Health System|language=en-US|access-date=2019-09-09}}</ref> 

In 2020, the molecular pathogen surveillance program Kasarskis had established with Dr. Harm van Bakel and others at the Mount Sinai Health System clearly demonstrated that [[SARS-CoV2]], the virus causing [[COVID-19]], was introduced to the [[New York metropolitan area|New York Metropolitan Area]] not from Asia but predominately from Europe, with some contribution from other United States regions.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/04/08/science/new-york-coronavirus-cases-europe-genomes.html |title=Most New York Coronavirus Cases Came From Europe, Genomes Show|website=New York Times|date=April 9, 2020|access-date=2021-06-25|last1=Zimmer|first1=Carl}}</ref> The ensuing research paper was published in the journal Science.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Introductions and early spread of SARS-CoV-2 in the New York City area|journal=Science|year=2020|doi=10.1126/science.abc1917|last1=Gonzalez-Reiche|first1=Ana S.|last2=Hernandez|first2=Matthew M.|last3=Sullivan|first3=Mitchell J.|last4=Ciferri|first4=Brianne|last5=Alshammary|first5=Hala|last6=Obla|first6=Ajay|last7=Fabre|first7=Shelcie|last8=Kleiner|first8=Giulio|last9=Polanco|first9=Jose|last10=Khan|first10=Zenab|last11=Alburquerque|first11=Bremy|last12=Van De Guchte|first12=Adriana|last13=Dutta|first13=Jayeeta|last14=Francoeur|first14=Nancy|last15=Melo|first15=Betsaida Salom|last16=Oussenko|first16=Irina|last17=Deikus|first17=Gintaras|last18=Soto|first18=Juan|last19=Sridhar|first19=Shwetha Hara|last20=Wang|first20=Ying-Chih|last21=Twyman|first21=Kathryn|last22=Kasarskis|first22=Andrew|last23=Altman|first23=Deena R.|last24=Smith|first24=Melissa|last25=Sebra|first25=Robert|last26=Aberg|first26=Judith|last27=Krammer|first27=Florian|last28=García-Sastre|first28=Adolfo|last29=Luksza|first29=Marta|last30=Patel|first30=Gopi|volume=369|issue=6501|pages=297–301|pmid=32471856|pmc=7259823|bibcode=2020Sci...369..297G|display-authors=1}}</ref>
